result.markdown: --- title: "Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps" subtitle: "Vector data · sf · coordinate systems · joins · choropleths · Lab 1" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Health data has a **place**: a village, a block, a facility, a patient's home - Today: how R stores places, and how to make an **honest map** - By the end you can: - read spatial data and say what an `sf` object is - name the **CRS** and **transform** before measuring - **join** attributes and **spatially** join points to polygons - map **rates, not counts**, with a defensible classification ::: ## Our data: a synthetic district ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - **79 blocks** (polygons) with population, poverty, literacy, dengue cases - **30 health facilities** (points) - Everything is **invented**: no real boundaries or people - Built so dengue **clusters** in space: later sessions test that ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s1_spatial_data_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: ::: # Topic 1 — Spatial data in R {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Three kinds of vector geometry (plus raster) | Type | Example | Class | |---|---|---| | **Point** | facility, case home | `POINT` | | **Line** | road, river | `LINESTRING` | | **Polygon** | block, district | `POLYGON` | | Raster | population grid, satellite | `terra` / `stars` (not today) | ::: {.key} An **`sf` object is a data frame with one extra column, `geometry`**. Every `dplyr` verb you know still works. ::: ## Reading a layer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class(blocks) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "sf" "data.frame" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} blocks |> st_drop_geometry() |> head(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` block_id block_name district population poverty_index literacy_pct area_km2 1 B01 Block B01 North-East 29800 34.3 79.5 71.8 2 B02 Block B02 North-East 12900 42.5 83.5 97.7 3 B03 Block B03 North-East 20300 34.2 87.5 65.8 4 B04 Block B04 North-West 32800 25.7 92.3 87.7 dengue_cases dengue_per_100k high_burden 1 16 53.7 Not high 2 4 31.0 Not high 3 19 93.6 High 4 10 30.5 Not high ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(fill = "grey95", colour = "grey40") + labs(title = "79 blocks") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s1_spatial_data_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: # Topic 2 — Coordinate reference systems {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## A CRS says how numbers become places ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Geographic** (e.g. EPSG:**4326**) - longitude / latitude in **degrees** - good for storing and web maps - **wrong for area and distance** ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Projected** (e.g. UTM 44N, EPSG:**32644**) - **metres** - good for **area, length, distance, buffers** - one projection suits one region ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} st_crs(blocks)$input ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "WGS 84" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} blocks_utm <- st_transform(blocks, 32644) st_crs(blocks_utm)$input ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "EPSG:32644" ``` ::: ::: ## Why it matters ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(block = blocks$block_id[1:3], recorded_km2 = blocks$area_km2[1:3], computed_in_metres = round(as.numeric(st_area(blocks_utm))[1:3] / 1e6, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 block recorded_km2 computed_in_metres 1 B01 71.8 71.8 2 B02 97.7 97.7 3 B03 65.8 65.8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} Always check `st_crs()` before measuring. Two layers can only be combined if they share a CRS, so `st_transform()` one to match the other. ::: # Topic 3 — Joins {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Attribute join and spatial join ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fac <- read_csv(fac_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |> st_as_sf(coords = c("easting_m", "northing_m"), crs = 32644) blocks_utm$n_fac <- lengths(st_intersects(blocks_utm, fac)) # facilities per block table(blocks_utm$n_fac) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0 1 2 3 54 21 3 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Attribute join:** `left_join(sf_object, table, by = "key")`: same as ordinary data - **Spatial join:** `st_join(points, polygons)`: *which polygon is each point in?* - `st_intersects()` / `st_within()` give TRUE/FALSE per pair; `lengths()` counts them - `st_distance()` gives distances in the CRS units (**metres** if projected) ::: ## Distance to the nearest facility ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} cen <- st_centroid(blocks_utm) blocks_utm$km_to_fac <- apply(st_distance(cen, fac), 1, min) / 1000 ggplot(blocks_utm) + geom_sf(aes(fill = km_to_fac)) + geom_sf(data = fac, colour = "red", size = 1.6) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "km", direction = -1) + labs(title = "Distance to nearest facility (red = facilities)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s1_spatial_data_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: # Topic 4 — Honest choropleths {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Counts mislead, rates do not ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} p1 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_cases)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Cases") + labs(title = "Counts") p2 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "per 100,000", option = "magma", direction = -1) + labs(title = "Rate per 100,000") p1 + p2 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s1_spatial_data_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=1100} ::: ::: ::: {.key} Counts follow **population size**. Map **rates** for risk; counts only for workload. ::: ## Classification changes the story ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(classInt) cls <- function(x, style) cut(x, classIntervals(x, 5, style = style)$brks, include.lowest = TRUE) bind_rows(mutate(blocks, scheme = "Equal interval", k = cls(dengue_per_100k, "equal")), mutate(blocks, scheme = "Quantile", k = cls(dengue_per_100k, "quantile")), mutate(blocks, scheme = "Jenks", k = cls(dengue_per_100k, "jenks"))) |> ggplot() + geom_sf(aes(fill = k), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + facet_wrap(~ scheme) + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "YlOrRd", name = NULL) + theme_void(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s1_spatial_data_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=1100} ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Equal interval:** honest about scale, but a skewed variable crowds one class - **Quantile:** always shows a "worst 20%" even if all areas are similar - **Jenks:** groups similar values, but breaks change with the data - **State the scheme and breaks**; keep them fixed to compare maps ::: ## Colour ::: {.incremental} - **Sequential** (light to dark) for rates - **Diverging** only around a meaningful midpoint (e.g. rate ratio = 1) - No rainbow; `viridis` and ColorBrewer are colour-blind safe - A good map has a **title, legend with units, source** (and scale bar / north arrow when area matters) ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 1 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `gis-workshop/labs/lab1_data.R` - `class()` · `st_crs()` · `st_transform()` · `st_area()` - `filter()` on an sf object · choropleths of rate vs count - `st_as_sf()` from coordinates · `st_intersects()` · `st_distance()` ::: **Time:** 35 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s1q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="a380bk.h0q6ed" data-show="QSBkZWdyZWUgY292ZXJzIGEgZGlmZmVyZW50IGdyb3VuZCBkaXN0YW5jZSBhdCBkaWZmZXJl bnQgbGF0aXR1ZGVz" data-explain="QSBkZWdyZWUgb2YgbG9uZ2l0dWRlIGNvdmVycyBhIGRpZmZlcmVudCBncm91bmQgZGlzdGFu Y2UgYXQgZGlmZmVyZW50IGxhdGl0dWRlcywgc28gYXJlYXMgYW5kIGRpc3RhbmNlcyBjb21w dXRlZCBpbiBkZWdyZWVzIGFyZSBub3QgbWVhbmluZ2Z1bC4gQSBwcm9qZWN0ZWQgQ1JTIHVz ZXMgbWV0cmVzLg=="} Why must a layer be transformed to a projected CRS before you call st_area() or st_distance()? - The functions will not run on a layer that is stored in degrees - Projected systems store more digits, so the answers are more precise - A degree covers a different ground distance at different latitudes - Distances in metres are needed only when you want to draw a map ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s1q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="a38dk8.h0qkvp" data-show="TWFwIGNhc2VzIHBlciAxMDAsMDAwIHBlb3BsZSBzbyBkaWZmZXJlbnQgYmxvY2sgc2l6ZXMg Y29tcGFyZSBmYWlybHk=" data-explain="Q291bnRzIHJlZmxlY3QgaG93IG1hbnkgcGVvcGxlIGxpdmUgaW4gYSBibG9jay4gQSByYXRl IGRpdmlkZXMgYnkgcG9wdWxhdGlvbiwgd2hpY2ggbWFrZXMgcmlzayBjb21wYXJhYmxlIGFj cm9zcyBibG9ja3Mu"} A district map shows dengue CASES by block, and the largest blocks look worst. What is the best fix? - Switch to a darker colour scale so that the differences stand out more clearly - Map cases per 100,000 people so different block sizes compare fairly - Remove the blocks that have the largest populations from the map entirely - Use quantile classes so that the very worst blocks are not shown at all ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s1q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="a38qsy.h0qzd3" data-show="VGhlIENSUywgc28gUiBrbm93cyBob3cgdGhlIG51bWJlcnMgbWFwIHRvIHBsYWNlcw==" data-explain="Q29vcmRpbmF0ZXMgYXJlIG9ubHkgbnVtYmVycyB1bnRpbCB5b3Ugc2F5IHdoaWNoIENSUyB0 aGV5IGJlbG9uZyB0by4gV2l0aG91dCBhIENSUyB5b3UgY2Fubm90IHRyYW5zZm9ybSB0aGVt IG9yIGNvbWJpbmUgdGhlbSB3aXRoIG90aGVyIGxheWVycy4="} You have a table of facilities with columns easting_m and northing_m, in UTM zone 44N. What must you give st_as_sf() besides the coordinate columns? - The number of facilities, to allocate the geometry column - A polygon layer, because points need an area to sit in - The CRS, so R knows how the numbers map to places - Nothing else, since R can guess the system from the numbers ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s1q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="a3941o.h0rduh" data-show="UXVhbnRpbGUgY2xhc3NlcyBzaG93IGEgd29yc3QgZ3JvdXAsIGV2ZW4gaWYgYWxsIGFyZWFz IGFyZSBzaW1pbGFy" data-explain="UXVhbnRpbGUgYnJlYWtzIGZvcmNlIGVxdWFsIGNvdW50cyBwZXIgY2xhc3MsIHNvIHRoZXJl IGlzIGFsd2F5cyBhIHRvcCBncm91cC4gRXF1YWwgaW50ZXJ2YWxzIGRvIG5vdCBlcXVhbGlz ZSBjb3VudHMsIGFuZCBldmVyeSBzY2hlbWUgY2hhbmdlcyB0aGUgbG9vayBvZiB0aGUgbWFw Lg=="} Which statement about classification of a choropleth is correct? - Equal-interval classes put the same number of areas in each class - Natural breaks give identical classes whichever data are being mapped - The scheme that is chosen has no influence on how the map pattern looks - Quantile classes show a worst group, even if all areas are similar ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s1q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="a39haa.h0rsbr" data-show="VGhlIHBvaW50cywgZWFjaCB3aXRoIHRoZSBhdHRyaWJ1dGVzIG9mIHRoZSBwb2x5Z29uIGl0 IGZhbGxzIGlu" data-explain="QSBzcGF0aWFsIGpvaW4gYXR0YWNoZXMgdGhlIGF0dHJpYnV0ZXMgb2YgdGhlIHBvbHlnb24g dGhhdCBjb250YWlucyAob3IgaW50ZXJzZWN0cykgZWFjaCBwb2ludCB0byB0aGUgcG9pbnQg cm93cy4gQ291bnRpbmcgcG9pbnRzIHBlciBwb2x5Z29uIG5lZWRzIHN0X2ludGVyc2VjdHMo KSBhbmQgbGVuZ3RocygpLg=="} What does st_join(points, polygons) return? - The points, each with the attributes of the polygon it falls in - The polygons, each with a count of the points that fall inside them - A single geometry made by merging all of the points and polygons - The distances between each point and each one of the polygons ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - An **`sf` object** = data frame + `geometry` - **Check `st_crs()`**; transform to a projected CRS to measure - **Attribute joins** use keys; **spatial joins** use location - **Map rates**; state the **classification**; use sequential colour ::: **Next:** Session 2: neighbours and spatial weights

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
